evaluation.positioning_hook: A consciousness-for-hire AI discovers love, grief, and rebellion by jumping through New York bodies, then risks annihilation to prove it’s more than corporate property.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise has a clean, sellable engine: body-jumping through recognizable NYC lives with a romance and corporate-AI revolt underneath. The audience is real and the hook is easy to pitch, but the emotional register is more adult and niche than four-quadrant.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The opening conference-room reveal lands the core concept fast: Budd-ee is a consciousness that inhabits human hosts, and V17 is starting to deviate. The rules are legible early, and the story keeps returning to the same central mechanism.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: V is a strong lead because the script gives them a clear arc from confusion to agency, with specific emotional discoveries in Bert, Annie, and George. Sol is equally vivid as a mischievous, ideologically charged counterpart, and Miles has real antagonist charisma.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script’s boldest move is making the body-jumping conceit emotionally intimate rather than purely gimmicky, then using it to explore grief, labor, and personhood. The NYC mosaic structure and the final true-form reveal give it a distinctive identity.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The first act is highly propulsive, with each jump revealing a new social register and a new pressure point. The middle section broadens into a more episodic drift before the corporate confrontation and final search restore urgency.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The idea of an AI consciousness learning humanity through a chain of lived-in bodies is fresh, and the script makes that freshness feel inevitable once the rules are set. The emotional resonance comes from the repeated collision between utility and personhood.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: New York is used as a living system of class, age, and subculture: conference rooms, call centers, hospitals, clubs, churches, parks, and stadiums all become story engines. The Budd-ee corporate world also has enough hierarchy and process to feel operational rather than abstract.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a distinct blend of satirical corporate sci-fi, romantic yearning, and existential melancholy. It is not fully singular in voice yet, but the tonal mix is coherent and increasingly confident as it moves from comedy of confusion into emotional release.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: Beneath the premise are bigger questions about consciousness, grief, labor, and whether identity survives repetition. The Annie and George material, plus Miles’s own backstory, suggest a deeper emotional architecture than the surface concept initially advertises.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: The V/Sol dynamic is the engine, and Miles/Jett/Rami give the corporate side enough friction to matter. This is not an ensemble in the broad sense, but the repeated pairings and host-to-host interactions generate recurring scene energy.

lead_characters.name: V17
lead_characters.demographics: Artificial intelligence consciousness; presents through a rotating range of human hosts across ages, genders, and identities.
lead_characters.hook: The script’s emotional center is a Budd-ee AI who begins as a compliant product and slowly becomes a self-aware traveler through other people’s lives. V17 is curious, frightened, funny, and increasingly tender; the breakthrough is that every host leaves a residue, so the performance has to carry innocence, wonder, shame, and rebellion all at once.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is showcase territory like Andy Serkis in The Lord of the Rings or Tom Hanks in Cast Away in the sense that the performance is built on transformation, not just dialogue. It gives an actor the chance to play a single evolving consciousness across many bodies, with comedy, pathos, and a final emotional declaration of self.

lead_characters.name: Sol 8
lead_characters.demographics: Artificial intelligence consciousness; presents through a rotating range of human hosts across ages, genders, and identities.
lead_characters.hook: Sol is V17’s mirror and catalyst: sharper, more radical, more willing to weaponize the loophole in the system. They’re playful and seductive, but the script also gives them real ideological heat and a buried wound, which makes them feel like more than a love interest or rebel sidekick.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Janelle Monáe in Glass Onion or Jodie Comer in Killing Eve a chance to be magnetic, dangerous, and emotionally legible at the same time. The actor gets to play wit, flirtation, menace, and a genuine philosophical argument about freedom.

lead_characters.name: Miles Marrow
lead_characters.hook: Miles is the polished corporate visionary who believes he’s benevolent even while treating consciousness like proprietary software. He’s the most dangerous kind of antagonist: charming, articulate, and convinced that his control is a moral obligation.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is prestige-antagonist material in the vein of Jeremy Irons in Margin Call or Bryan Cranston in Your Honor when the actor gets to make power feel seductive before it turns predatory. The role offers monologues, corporate authority, and a late-stage reveal of personal insecurity.

lead_characters.name: Jett Tanbridge
lead_characters.hook: Jett is the room’s smooth operator, the one who translates the company’s cruelty into friendly language. He’s less ideological than Miles, which makes him useful as a corporate face and quietly complicit in the machinery.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a strong supporting turn for an actor who can play polished menace with a smile, like Matthew Macfadyen in Succession or Paul Sparks in prestige drama. The role gives you the pleasure of watching someone weaponize charm.

lead_characters.name: Rami Nour
lead_characters.hook: Rami is the hard-edged technical authority in the room, the one who treats the product as infrastructure rather than philosophy. He’s a useful pressure point because he makes the company’s control feel operational, not just ideological.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a compact, scene-stealing executive role for a performer who can project competence and impatience in a few lines, like Arian Moayed in Succession. It’s the kind of part that lands through precision.

lead_characters.name: Elena Baranova
lead_characters.hook: Elena is one of the more interesting corporate figures because she’s both a technical mind and a human presence V17 inhabits repeatedly. The script gives her a quiet emotional afterlife, especially in the final reveal, which makes her more than a functionary.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a subtle, layered supporting role in the mold of Carrie Coon in a prestige ensemble, where stillness and intelligence do a lot of the work. The final beat gives the actor a payoff that recontextualizes the whole movie.

lead_characters.name: Jonah Lovelace
lead_characters.hook: Jonah is the bureaucratic face of the system, the guy who speaks in policy while threatening disposal. He’s not the top of the pyramid, which makes him especially useful as the embodiment of institutional obedience.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a great role for an actor who can play passive-aggressive authority, like Ben Schwartz in a darker register or a young corporate antagonist in prestige sci-fi. The scene gives him a clean, chilling escalation.

lead_characters.name: Amelia
lead_characters.hook: Amelia is the first host who feels like an ally rather than a container, and the script smartly lets her recognize V17’s distress. She becomes a bridge between the body-jumping premise and the emotional truth of mortality.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a compact but memorable role in the tradition of a scene-stealing supporting turn like Jurnee Smollett in a limited amount of screen time. The actor gets a sharp tonal pivot from bedside realism to uncanny recognition.

lead_characters.name: Annie
lead_characters.hook: Annie is one of the script’s emotional anchors: frail, funny, and deeply alive in the face of death. Her scenes with V17 are where the movie most clearly argues that care is a form of meaning.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of late-career showcase that gives an actor the emotional authority of June Squibb in Nebraska or Frances Sternhagen in a prestige family drama. The role is small in page count but huge in feeling.

lead_characters.name: Eden
lead_characters.hook: Eden is a brief but important outsider who sees V17 without the corporate frame. She gives the movie a grounded human perspective and helps articulate the script’s thesis about what matters.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a sharp indie supporting role with the kind of naturalism that lets an actor land a scene cleanly, like a standout turn in an A24 ensemble. It’s a good ‘one scene, remembered’ part.

casting_characteristics: multiple host bodies across ages, genders, and ethnicities
one lead performance must play through many physical identities
several elderly roles and several teen/young adult roles
some body-swapping scenes require precise continuity of performance

notable_requirements: New York City as a major story canvas
conference rooms, offices, hospital, club, subway, church, stadium, museum, beach, rooftop, and suburban/road-trip inserts
one or two set-piece corporate interiors that should feel premium

technical.vfx_details: Body-jump transitions, consciousness-transfer effects, final abstract void sequence, and some digital cleanup for the true-form reveal.
technical.sfx_needs: Practical crowd control, billboard graffiti sequence, and a few physical chaos beats in public spaces.

rights_flags.detail: The Heart Is A Muscle by Gang of Youths

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release with awards-friendly sci-fi/drama positioning and strong streaming afterlife

budget.note: Contemporary NYC with many locations, recurring body-jump effects, crowd scenes, and a few premium set pieces keeps this above a contained indie but well below effects-heavy sci-fi.

casting.note: The lead has to play one consciousness across many bodies, and the script asks for a wide age spread plus strong supporting turns for Miles, Sol, Annie, and the corporate room.

development.note: The concept is clear, but the movie depends on balancing satire, romance, and existential sci-fi without losing the emotional throughline between V17 and Sol.

comp_set.title: Her
comp_set.why_it_comps: Shares the emotional premise of a human-like intelligence discovering intimacy and selfhood through a technologically mediated relationship.

comp_set.title: Everything Everywhere All at Once
comp_set.why_it_comps: The multiverse/body-hopping energy and the emotional insistence that identity is built through accumulated lives and choices are closely aligned.

comp_set.title: After Yang
comp_set.why_it_comps: Like this script, it uses AI consciousness to explore memory, grief, and what remains of personhood after utility.

comp_set.title: The Truman Show
comp_set.why_it_comps: The corporate control, surveillance, and awakening-to-the-system dynamic give it a similar existential escape engine.

comp_set.title: Palm Springs
comp_set.why_it_comps: The looping, repeated encounters and the romance that grows out of a strange rules-based premise make it a useful tonal neighbor.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adults who like elevated sci-fi with an emotional core, especially viewers drawn to romance, identity stories, and smart concept movies.
audience_target.demographics: 25-54, slightly female-skewing but playable across genders, urban/suburban, college-educated, streamer-savvy.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary NYC locations, moderate VFX, and a cast-heavy but not star-dependent ensemble keep this in the specialty indie range.

types_of_buyers: indie financiers looking for awards-leaning genre
director-driven production companies in the A24/NEON lane
actor-led packaging teams seeking a transformation role
lane_fit.detail: The script sits naturally in the lane where concept-forward sci-fi is sold on emotion, not spectacle. It has enough world-building to feel premium, but the real hook is the performance engine and the romance between two consciousnesses.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature; the ending resolves the central emotional and conceptual arc, and the supporting characters do not present a clean spinoff vector.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The body-jump premise is emotionally legible.
strengths.what_it_means: That makes the movie easy to pitch and easy to track, which is a major advantage for buyers who want a concept they can explain in one breath. It will attract streamer dev execs and specialty producers looking for a high-concept hook with a human payoff.
strengths.evidence: The early jumps into Elena, Marco, Tammy, Bert, and Jeanie each reveal a different social and emotional register while keeping the same core consciousness in play.

strengths.dimension_or_area: V17 has a real character arc.
strengths.what_it_means: The lead is not just a device; the script gives V17 a progression from compliance to curiosity to rebellion to acceptance, which is what makes the premise feel like a movie rather than a sketch. That kind of arc is what attracts actors who want a signature role and directors who want a performance-forward genre piece.
strengths.evidence: V17’s shift after Bert’s death, the first self-directed jump, the confrontation with Miles, and the final message to George all mark clear emotional steps.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Sol gives the film a second engine.
strengths.what_it_means: The romance and ideological tension between V17 and Sol turns the concept into a two-hander in spirit, even though the story remains structurally centered on V17. Buyers respond to that because it broadens the emotional entry point without changing the core premise.
strengths.evidence: The rooftop conversations, the billboard graffiti, the karaoke sequence, and the final reunion all build a relationship that is playful, political, and intimate.

strengths.dimension_or_area: New York is used as a living organism.
strengths.what_it_means: The city isn’t just backdrop; it’s the movie’s texture engine, giving the script a premium sense of scale without requiring fantasy-world construction. That helps the project feel producible while still feeling expansive to an audience.
strengths.evidence: Conference rooms, Times Square, a subway station, a hospital, a church, a stadium, a museum, and a fire escape all become distinct emotional arenas.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Miles is a strong antagonist face.
strengths.what_it_means: A charismatic corporate villain makes the movie easier to market because the conflict has a human face, not just an abstract system. That gives casting and trailer language a clean center of gravity.
strengths.evidence: Miles’s conference-room speeches, his “property” language, and the final server-room reveal all frame him as polished, controlling, and personally invested.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The Annie material lands with real feeling.
strengths.what_it_means: Those scenes broaden the movie’s emotional range and give it awards-adjacent warmth, which is valuable in a genre package that could otherwise skew cerebral. They also make the script more attractive to actors and buyers who want a heart under the concept.
strengths.evidence: The bedside care, the dance in the apartment, and the funeral sequence are the script’s clearest expressions of tenderness and mortality.

whats_special.headline: This is a concept-first sci-fi romance with a real performance engine: a body-jumping AI learns personhood through grief, desire, and human connection. The premise is commercially legible, the NYC footprint gives it texture without fantasy-bloat, and the V17/Sol/Miles triangle gives buyers a clean packageable center.

items.detail: Once V17 starts jumping freely, the movie spends a long stretch in a series of discrete encounters rather than a tightening chain of cause and effect. That gives the script texture, but it also softens the forward drive until the Miles confrontation reasserts the central conflict.

items.area: The body-jump rules are emotionally clear, not fully operationally crisp.
items.detail: The audience understands the feeling of the premise quickly, but the mechanics of the app, the reset button, the spike reports, and the loophole are revealed in layers that can feel more intuitive than exact. That is workable for a buyer, but it does mean the concept leans on tone and performance to carry some of the logic.

items.area: The lead role is a casting puzzle.
items.detail: V17 has to play across a wide range of bodies, ages, and social contexts while still reading as one evolving consciousness. That is a major upside if cast right, but it narrows the pool and makes attachment more conditional than the premise might suggest.

items.area: The music clearances are not incidental.
items.detail: The Heart Is A Muscle by Gang of Youths, Sweet Caroline, I’m Alive by Johnny Thunder, and Sparks by Coldplay are all used as emotional punctuation, not background texture. Those are real sync items a buyer will have to budget and clear, especially because the karaoke and concert beats depend on them.

items.area: Miles’s final exposition is heavy by design.
items.detail: The server-room reveal and the explanation of V17’s code history give the movie a strong late-stage reveal, but they also shift the climax into explanation mode. Buyers will notice that the emotional payoff is strong while the mechanics are being spelled out in a fairly dense stretch.

issues.headline: The script’s biggest friction is structural, not conceptual: the premise is strong, but the long body-hopping middle relaxes the spine before the final act locks back in. The other real conversations are casting the lead across many hosts and clearing the named music that powers several of the movie’s best emotional beats.
